query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small reactive element (e.g., 2 atomic percent yttrium) to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will form fine, stable oxide dispersoids at the grain boundaries during high-temperature exposure, thereby improving the alloy’s creep resistance and high-temperature strength compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy composed of titanium and nickel as primary constituents plus three other elements (each present at 5–35 at%) in a homogeneous, equiaxed grain structure.
generation.intervention: Microalloying with 2 at% yttrium (Y) added to the standard alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature testing in the range of 600°C to 800°C under oxidizing atmospheres to promote in situ oxidation of yttrium.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of finely dispersed Y2O3 oxide particles at grain boundaries and within the grains.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures and in an oxidizing environment, yttrium oxidizes preferentially to form stable, nanometer-scale Y2O3 particles. These oxide dispersoids act as pinning points that retard grain boundary sliding and inhibit dislocation motion, thereby increasing the alloy’s resistance to creep and overall high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The yttrium-doped alloy will exhibit lower creep rates and higher tensile strength at elevated temperatures (e.g., 700°C) than the control alloy lacking yttrium. Improvements are expected to be on the order of a 10–30% increase in performance, though the exact improvement may vary.
generation.baseline: The same titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without yttrium addition.
generation.boundary: Alloy compositions satisfying the high-entropy definition in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents, tested between 600°C and 800°C in oxidizing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While oxide dispersion strengthening is well established in other alloy families (e.g., ODS steels), its quantitative impact and stability in titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys are not well characterized. Variability in oxide particle size, distribution, and the overall interactions with the matrix at these compositions contribute to uncertainty in the magnitude of improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy: one set with a 2 at% yttrium addition and one set without (control). Process both sets under identical casting and thermomechanical treatments and then subject them to high-temperature exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere at 700°C.
measurements: Creep rate under a constant load at 700°C
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to detect and characterize Y2O3 oxide dispersoids and grain boundary morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., reduction in creep rate and/or increase in tensile strength at 700°C in repeated tests) compared to the control, or if microstructural analysis does not confirm the formation of fine Y2O3 dispersoids, then the hypothesis is falsified.
